title: The Salt Caravan
summary: On the long road to the salt pans, a young driver learns that a grudge weighs more than any load of salt.
moral: Share the water; the desert will take the grudge anyway.
attribution: A traditional Hausa tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: Camels carrying salt blocks across rolling dunes towards a low sun, with patterned cloth bands above

sentences.text: The salt caravan left the town before first light, when the air was still cool and the camels complained softly under their loads.
It would travel for many days to the pans, and many days back, and the success of the journey was measured by two things: the salt that arrived, and the people who did.
A young driver named Suleiman had been given charge of two camels and a share of the water.
He was proud of this.
He walked beside his camels with the rope over his shoulder and looked at the older drivers to see how they did it.
At the noon halt on the third day, he noticed that his family’s old rival, Danladi, was waterless.
Danladi’s skin bag had split.
He was sitting in the shade of his camel, not asking anyone for help, and the other drivers were looking elsewhere.
Suleiman’s father had told him never to help Danladi, because of a debt from before Suleiman was born.
Suleiman looked at his own full bag, and then at the old man’s dry mouth, and then at the long road ahead, which did not care about debts.
He carried the water over and let Danladi drink.
Danladi stared at him a long time and then said, “Your father will hear of this.”
Suleiman said, “My father has not walked this road in ten years.
I have.”
The caravan moved on that afternoon with a lighter silence.
At the pans, when the salt was loaded, the caravan leader took Suleiman aside.
“You wondered why I put you beside Danladi,” he said.
“The desert does not care whose grandfather quarrelled with whose.
Water shared is water saved.
The heaviest load on the road to the salt pans is a grudge, and you put yours down.”
